title: Reply to Kettl: Public Administration and the Shifting Competing Forces of Accountability
authors: Charles Wise
affiliations: School of Government and Public Policy University of Arizona Tucson Arizona USA
abstract: ABSTRACT The accountability context for how public administrators operate has shifted markedly and has become much more volatile. This shift has placed new and some conflicting demands on public administrators to demonstrate their accountability to various competing governmental actors and has complicated policy and program implementation. The changed context, its causes, and the resultant challenges are analyzed and discussed. Questions are presented for public administration research to help public administrators deal with the challenges.

title: Public Interest Capacity: The Case of Direct File
authors: Donald Moynihan; Pam Herd; Xiaoyang Xu
affiliations: Ford School of Public Policy University of Michigan Ann Arbor Michigan USA; Department of Political Science University of South Carolina Columbia South Carolina USA
abstract: ABSTRACT This article describes the conditions for creating and undermining public interest capacity, that is, the ability of the state to generate public goods with widely distributed benefits. The creation and elimination of Direct File, a free, online public tax reporting system in the United States, offers an instrumental case. The creation of Direct File depended upon political commitment sufficient to overcome private interests: both the traditional dependence on private contractors to produce digital products, and the opposition of the private tax preparation industry which saw Direct File as a competitor. Political will was not enough: creating internal capacity in the form of skilled government tech teams who could build a quality digital product was also necessary. But without this political commitment in the Trump administration, which instead pursued downsizing and was receptive to the tax preparation industry arguments, both Direct File and the team that built it were eliminated.

title: Colleagues that work together move together: How co-moving among newcomers affects individual and team performance.
authors: Emma Y. Zhao; Catherine Shea; Siyuan Li
affiliations: University of Virginia, McIntire School of Commerce, Charlottesville, Virginia, United States; Carnegie Mellon University Tepper School of Business, Organizational Behavior and Theory, Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, United States; William & Mary Raymond A Mason School of Business, Mason School of Business, Williamsburg, Virginia, United States
abstract: As teams and team membership become more dynamic, colleagues from the same prior team increasingly transition together to a new team as a cohort: a phenomenon known as co-moving. Drawing on theories of shared team experience and team receptivity, we develop a multilevel, multi-theory, and multi-period model to examine how co-moving affects individual and team performance. We theorize that co-movers carry forward proximal shared team experience which they can leverage immediately to support their own performance relative to solo movers, who must build new working relationships. However, we also theorize that co-movers’ proximal shared team experience hinders team performance, though these detrimental effects attenuate over time. We test our theory using archival data from the National Basketball Association, supplemented by qualitative interviews with individuals involved in professional basketball. Our findings reveal that co-movers exhibit better individual performance than solo movers on their new teams and in our robustness checks we find that greater shared tenure on the prior team further enhances this advantage. At the team level, teams with co-movers perform worse than teams with solo movers, and we find partial support that this disadvantage attenuates over time. Additional analyses show that co-movers’ individual performance advantage persists over time in the new team. The findings from our interviews illuminate how these processes unfold both on and off the court. Our research contributes to the literature on shared team experience and newcomer integration by highlighting a multilevel tradeoff: while co-moving benefits individuals, it can initially undermine collective performance.

title: Legal Chameleons: Political Ideology, Institutional Histories, and Firms’ Management of Identity Cues
authors: Yong Kim; Jose Nicolas Uribe; Maxim Sytch
affiliations: Texas A&M University, Department of Management, College Station, Texas, United States; Indiana University, Management and Entrepreneurship, Bloomington, Indiana, United States; University of Michigan-Ann Arbor, Management and Organizations, Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States
abstract: This study examines how foreign firms strategically manage the salience of foreignness when facing unfavorable domestic evaluators. Foreign firms do so by altering the ethnic composition of the agents representing them before the evaluators. We examine this question in the context of Asian firms’ selection of legal counsel in U.S. federal courts. Prior research suggests that foreign firms may anticipate less favorable evaluations in courts that have historically favored domestic over foreign firms and in those with conservative judges. We argue that, in such evaluative settings, Asian firms adjust the ethnic composition of their external legal teams to manage the salience of foreignness, and that such adjustments are especially likely in courts that combine judge conservatism with pro-domestic ruling histories. We test these arguments using data on U.S. patent litigation from 2000 to 2016 and validated measures of courts’ political ideology and pro-domestic ruling histories. We find that Asian firms reduce the proportion of Asian-origin lawyers and increase the proportion of White lawyers when litigating in conservative courts, particularly when these courts also have pro-domestic ruling histories. By contrast, the ethnic composition of lawyers representing domestic firms remains stable across courts. Evidence of implicit bias against Asians among legal professionals provides additional support consistent with the theorized mechanism. Post-hoc analyses reveal that adjusting the ethnic composition of external legal teams attenuates the likelihood of unfavorable outcomes in conservative courts. These findings contribute to research on liability of foreignness by identifying agent selection as a specific mitigation mechanism in evaluative arenas.

title: Reconceptualizing Network Change: Robustness and Resilience of Interorganizational Networks
authors: Maxim Sytch; Sukanya Roy; Pavel I. Zhelyazkov
affiliations: University of Michigan, Management and Organizations, Ross School of Business, Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States; University of Michigan, Ross School of Business, Management and Organizations, Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States; The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Management, Kowloon, Hong Kong
abstract: Existing research on interorganizational network dynamics has largely treated network change as gradual, local, and primarily oriented toward private organizational advantage. Yet contemporary cooperative interorganizational systems are highly interconnected across industrial sectors and geographies and are routinely exposed to shocks that simultaneously disable multiple organizations or relationships among them. These shocks stem from pandemics, natural disasters, wars, sanctions, and cascading partner failures, and can rapidly reconfigure whole‑network architectures and undermine collective outcomes. In light of this new reality, we reconceptualize interorganizational networks as loci of frequent, punctuated change at the whole network level, with primary implications for collective outcomes. We develop this reconceptualization through a robustness–resilience lens, defining network robustness as an interorganizational network’s capacity to maintain its collective outcomes in the immediate aftermath of a shock, and network resilience as its capacity to recover and potentially surpass pre‑shock collective outcomes over the longer term. We then outline the theoretical and methodological opportunities that this robustness–resilience perspective opens for the study of network change.

title: Collective Activism
authors: Craig Doidge; Alexander Dyck; Liyan Yang
affiliations: Rotman School of Management, University of Toronto, Toronto, Ontario M5S3E6, Canada
abstract: Can investor stewardship codes that call for coordinated activism be satisfied by an Investor Collective Action Organization (ICAO)? In an ICAO, investors work collectively, like a large shareholder, to monitor management and increase value. We analyze the endogenous formation of an ICAO and its equilibrium size, considering free-rider problems and coordination costs. While the ICAO overcomes free-rider problems among its members, it exacerbates them between the ICAO and solo activists. The benefit of joining an ICAO is hump-shaped in size. With moderate coordination costs, ICAO formation features multiple equilibria. Small changes in coordination costs significantly influence ICAO formation and activism. This paper was accepted by Will Cong, finance. Funding: L. title: Quality Regulation and Competition: Evidence from Pharmaceutical Markets
authors: Juan Pablo Atal; José Ignacio Cuesta; Morten Sæthre
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania and NBER; Stanford University and NBER; Norwegian School of Economics
abstract: Abstract Quality regulation seeks to ensure quality and foster competition by reducing vertical differentiation, but it may also have adverse effects on market structure. We study this trade-off in the context of pharmaceutical bioequivalence, which is the primary quality standard for generic drugs. By exploiting the introduction of bioequivalence in Chile, we find that stronger regulation reduced the number of drugs in the market by 18% and increased average paid prices by 13%. We estimate a model of drug entry, certification, and demand to study how drug quality, aversion to generics, and certification costs shape the equilibrium effects of quality regulation. We find that quality regulation increased demand for generic drugs by resolving asymmetric information and reducing aversion to unbranded generics, which induced the entry of high-quality drugs in place of low-quality drugs. Consumer welfare increased despite higher prices and a lower number of firms. We compare minimum quality standards with alternative designs of quality regulation, including quality disclosure.

title: ‘This is not what science is’: Researchers’ perspectives on doing decolonial research in Flemish (Belgian) higher education
authors: Elif Lootens; Peter A. J. Stevens; Bart Van de Putte
affiliations: Ghent University, Belgium
abstract: Despite the sociological attention paid to the role of racism in producing racial inequalities in universities, few studies have examined epistemic coloniality and marginalization at the level of social knowledge within academia. Foregrounding the university context, where anti-colonial knowledge is simultaneously marginalized, this article asks what the possibilities are for decolonial critiques of knowledge within universities. Based on interviews with racialized PhD researchers of colour, this study examines the possibilities and challenges of conducting decolonial research within a university context. We argue that the epistemic frameworks of social sciences are intrinsically racialized, fostering exclusionary modes of thought and practices that align with racial and socio-geographical lines. Second, this study reveals how dominant conceptions of scientific validity and neutrality in social sciences sustain the epistemic status quo, contributing to ‘epistemic coloniality’ by invalidating decolonial researchers.

title: Modeling collective action in POM: The Strategy–Operations–People framework
authors: Guillaume Roels; Ludo Van der Heyden
affiliations: INSEAD
abstract: While many business situations relevant to production and operations management (POM), such as supply chain coordination or sustainable operations, involve some form of collective action; managerial frameworks for collective action rarely appear in POM contexts. Valuable insights may thus be missed, reducing the effectiveness and implementability of the proposed POM solutions. To bridge this gap, this paper presents a framework for collective action that has its roots in the organizational behavior literature. We formalize it mathematically not only to offer definitional clarity, but also to relate it to common POM modeling approaches. We then illustrate its relevance to POM by mapping it to case studies in supply chain coordination and sustainable operations. The proposed framework, named the Strategy–Operations–People (SOP) framework, is structured in three levels, comprising three elements, two elements, and one element, respectively. First, the Strategy level induces and enforces solidarity among all team members by specifying common goals, shared values, and well-defined rules. Second, the Operations level organizes the decentralized execution of collective action in autonomous subgroups through a detailed specification of roles and processes. Third, the People level requires the individual commitment of all team members to the proposed collective action program, since a team’s performance rests on the individual contributions of its members. The framework thus addresses the common, subgroup, and individual dimensions of collective action. The SOP framework also contributes to the broader fields of team leadership and organizational behavior in two ways. First, its mathematical formalization brings operational clarity on the defining scope of the framework’s elements. Second, mapping the framework to two problems in supply chain management and sustainable operations illustrates its broad applicability, moving beyond collective action within organizations, to guide collective action taking place across organizations.

title: How Strategic Leaders Drive Firms in Ecosystems: Envisioning Value, Orchestrating Knowledge, and Shifting Roles
authors: Paolo Aversa; Carmelo Cennamo; Ambra Mazzelli; Gianni Lorenzoni
affiliations: King's College London; Copenhagen Business School; SKEMA Business School, Université Côte d'Azur (GREDEG); University of Bologna
abstract: Abstract Research on business ecosystems has illuminated how ecosystems emerge, evolve, and transform, revealing ecosystem‐level dynamics and the central actors that orchestrate them. Yet, it is individual firms that continuously attempt to establish and shift the roles they play within ecosystems through the vision and choices of their strategic leaders. How do strategic leaders drive these shifts? Through a longitudinal case study of Dallara Automobili (1972–2025), we trace how the CEO's prior professional experience shaped an evolving theory of value – a set of conjectures about how value should be created that guided the development of organizational routines enabling progressively more expansive knowledge orchestration. This process shifted Dallara from a peripheral component supplier to a boundary‐spanning knowledge orchestrator. Our recursive process model theorizes how the leader's conjectures drive firm role shifts within an ecosystem: experience shapes the leader's theory of value, which drives organizational routines and knowledge orchestration; knowledge orchestration, in turn, redefines the firm's ecosystem role. Ecosystem responses then feed back, augmenting prior experience and, in turn, refining the theory of value so that each round operates at a broader scope. We contribute to ecosystem research by identifying knowledge orchestration as the mechanism through which a leader's theory of value translates into shifts in the firm's role and by showing how this process unfolds recursively as ecosystem responses reshape the leader's conjectures.

title: Generative AI and Firm Values
authors: ANDREA L. EISFELDT; GREGOR SCHUBERT; MIAO BEN ZHANG; BLEDI TASKA
abstract: ABSTRACT How do recent advances in Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) affect firm value? We construct the first measure of firms' workforce exposures to Generative AI and show that an “Artificial‐Minus‐Human” portfolio earned 5% in the two weeks following the release of ChatGPT. The labor‐exposure effect is more pronounced for firms with greater data assets and is distinct from the effect of firms' product exposures to AI. We assess whether exposed workforces are substituted or complemented by Generative AI based on whether their exposed tasks are core or supplemental. Examining firms' labor demand and profitability following the release of ChatGPT supports a labor‐technology substitution channel.

title: The Depositary of Last Resort
authors: Pamfili Antipa; Kilian Rieder
affiliations: London School of Economics and Political Science . Houghton St, London WC2A 2AE,; Oesterreichische Nationalbank (Eurosystem) & CEPR . Otto-Wagner-Platz 3, 1090 Vienna,
abstract: Abstract What are the consequences of making central bank deposits accessible to actors beyond the banking sector? We collect novel micro data on deposit accounts historically held with the Bank of England by individuals and firms other than banks to study their role in the financial panic of 1866. We document that the use of deposit accounts at the central bank soared during the crisis, while commercial banks permanently lost funding. The expansion in the number of active accounts was fueled by individuals, but the intensive margin increase in balances came almost entirely from firms. Recourse to central bank deposits was heterogeneous and persisted well beyond the panic, reflecting easy access, low opportunity costs, and positive network externalities. At the same time, retail borrowers seeking liquidity support from the Bank during the crisis preferred receiving loan proceeds in the form of cash rather than deposits. title: Building Better Information: Reporting Technology, Internal Information Frictions, and Investment Efficiency
authors: Philip G. Berger; Feng Li; Lisa Yao Liu; M. H. Franco Wong
affiliations: The University of Chicago; Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Columbia University; University of California, Irvine
abstract: ABSTRACT We assess how firms use spending on reporting infrastructure to improve managerial reporting quality (MRQ) and whether doing so improves investment efficiency. Using the Sarbanes-Oxley Act’s internal control provisions (SOX 404) as a shock to MRQ demand, we find that treated firms increase reporting infrastructure spending, including for information technology and communications. We next examine variation across segments in the benefits and costs of improving reporting infrastructure. Segments increase spending more when facing larger internal moral hazard frictions and when they are less likely to have voluntarily improved MRQ before SOX (including segments insulated from competition, facing difficulty obtaining enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems, or lacking internal control personnel). Finally, we find that treated firms improve investment efficiency post-SOX 404, with larger gains among firms with higher spending on reporting infrastructure. Our findings indicate that regulatory mandates can improve investment efficiency by inducing reporting infrastructure improvements that enhance MRQ. title: Social Media Toxicity and Capital Markets
authors: Elizabeth Blankespoor; Jedson Pinto; Kirti Sinha
affiliations: University of Washington; The University of Texas at Dallas
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper asks about the existence, determinants, and implications of toxic content in financial social media. Using machine learning algorithms to measure toxicity in Seeking Alpha articles and comments, we find measurable toxicity concentrated primarily in user-generated comments rather than articles. Comment toxicity is greater for firms with more investor attention or uncertainty. We document three key results about toxicity in capital markets. First, toxicity displays a feedback loop in platform participation: past toxicity is associated with more future toxic contributors for a given firm. Second, firms receiving more toxic comments have greater retail trading volume but less informative retail trades, especially when comments disagree. Third, toxicity is associated with slower price discovery around earnings announcements. Our findings suggest that financial social media toxicity relates to both user behavior and market outcomes and raise important considerations for platform governance in financial markets. Data Availability: The Seeking Alpha articles and comments used in this study were obtained directly from Seeking Alpha under a data-sharing arrangement and are proprietary; we are not permitted to redistribute them. These data may be requested from Seeking Alpha. Compustat, Execucomp, CRSP, and New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) Trade and Quote (TAQ) data are available through Wharton Research Data Services (WRDS) to subscribing institutions. title: So similar, yet so different: comparing the US GAAP and IFRS experience at eliciting greater transparency on pension asset disclosures
authors: Divya Anantharaman; Elizabeth Chuk; Tonni Shijun Xia
abstract: Abstract We exploit two regulatory changes, one under US GAAP and the other under IFRS, that mandate improved disclosure of pension asset allocation. While the changes are otherwise similar, US GAAP retains the expected rate of return (“ERR”) on pension assets, which preparers can more easily manipulate if asset allocation remains opaque, while IFRS eliminates the ERR. We find that the IFRS standard improves pension asset transparency more than the US standard, which only mandates higher-quality disclosure without changing recognition or measurement and hence leaves unchanged preparers’ incentives to obfuscate. The US standard elicits a mixed response that reduces transparency in some respects. We isolate the relative deterioration in US firms’ transparency to firms with stronger incentives to inflate ERRs. Overall, our study highlights the potential for standard setters to learn from each other by comparing their regulatory experience on a specific accounting topic with clearly identifiable managerial incentives.
